claims.text: Controlled surface annealing in a mildly oxidizing environment will produce a thin, adherent oxide layer on the HEA.
The annealing-generated oxide layer will be lubricious.
The oxide layer will lower the coefficient of friction across a wide service-temperature range.
The oxide layer will lower the wear rate across a wide service-temperature range.
Annealing in a controlled low-oxygen atmosphere at an optimized temperature and duration will promote in situ formation of a nanocrystalline, potentially spinel-type surface oxide.
Annealing at 600–700 °C is high enough to initiate selective surface oxidation.
A sufficient annealing duration will produce a continuous oxide layer.
Rapid cooling after annealing will retain the HEA microstructure.
The treatment will form a sub-micron nanocrystalline oxide film.
The oxide film will act as a solid lubricant between the sliding surfaces.
The oxide film will reduce friction by providing a low-shear-strength interface.
The oxide film will reduce wear by protecting the underlying HEA from direct mechanical contact.
The oxide film will remain stable from room temperature to approximately 800 °C if it stays intact and adherent.
Treatment will reduce the coefficient of friction by an estimated 20–30% relative to the untreated alloy across the service-temperature interval.
Treatment will reduce the wear rate by an estimated 20–30% relative to the untreated alloy across the service-temperature interval.
The untreated alloy has higher friction than the treated alloy.
The untreated alloy has higher wear than the treated alloy.
Film spallation under mechanical stress can eliminate or diminish the treatment's tribological benefit.
Further oxidation or reduction above approximately 800 °C can degrade the oxide film and its tribological performance.
Prolonged cyclic loading can degrade the oxide film and its tribological performance.
